LESSON 4 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

Assets, Threats, Vulnerabilities & Risk

The four words that carry all of security: define assets, threats, vulnerabilities and risk, and see how they combine into the risk equation defenders actually use.

Beginner15 min
Why this matters

Asset, threat, vulnerability and risk are four different ideas that get used interchangeably. Keeping them separate is what makes risk assessment possible rather than an exercise in worry.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • An asset is anything of value that an attacker would want: data, hardware, credentials, availability, or your reputation.
  • A threat is a potential cause of harm, from an external attacker to an insider mistake to a hardware fault.
  • A vulnerability is a weakness that a threat could exploit. Not every vulnerability is exploitable, and not every exploit needs a vulnerability you knew about.
  • Risk is the combination of likelihood and impact. It is what you are actually trying to reduce.
  • Risk equals threat times vulnerability times exposure. Removing any one of the three is usually cheaper than adding another control.

The background

  • The vocabulary comes from risk management traditions in insurance and safety engineering, and was borrowed by computing in the 1970s.
  • Early systems treated risk informally; formal methods such as fault trees, attack trees and the National Information Assurance Academy glossary formalised the language.
  • Modern practice adds likelihood scoring and business impact, so that a technical finding can be ranked against cost and effort.
  • The FAIR and NIST approaches differ in detail, but both insist that risk is about the business, not only about the technology.

Real-world examples

  • An unpatched web server is a vulnerability; an attacker who scans for it is a threat; the combination is the risk that decides patch timing.
  • The same vulnerability in an isolated lab and in an internet-facing production host is a completely different risk, because exposure differs.
  • A medium-severity finding can outrank a critical one when it affects the only system the business can serve from.

What to look for

  • Build the asset list before scanning, so findings are ranked by what they actually threaten.
  • Record exposure: reachable from the internet, reachable by staff, or reachable only by administrators.
  • Separate a theoretical weakness from a demonstrated exploit path before prioritising work.
  • Note the compensating controls that already reduce likelihood.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — triage drill

Open CISA resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Maintain an asset inventory with an owner for each entry.
  • Rank findings by risk, not by scanner severity, and record the reason for each deferral.
  • Track exposure separately from vulnerability so reducing reach is visible as progress.
  • Revisit the assessment when the system changes, not only on a fixed calendar.
